name: Fujimorism
summary: Fujimorism is the political current of Alberto Fujimori's presidency of Peru (1990-2000) and the Fuerza Popular movement that carries his name. It combines a hard-line, order-first presidency that dissolved Congress in the 1992 self-coup and ruled through a strong executive, with a free-market programme of austerity, privatisation and trade opening, anti-insurgent security policy and outreach to the poor through direct appeals rather than parties.
scope: The government of Alberto Fujimori (1990-2000) and the 1993 constitution adopted under it, as the scholarship on 'el fujimorismo' (García Montero, Díaz-Terán) and Britannica describe them. The party platforms of Fuerza Popular under Keiko Fujimori and Kenji Fujimori's breakaway faction are not the basis of any answer.

sources.usedFor: Names the 1993 constitution as the institutional legacy of Fujimori's government; background for scope.

ban-cartels.rationale: The constitution has the State fight any practice that limits free competition and bars any law or arrangement from authorising monopolies (art. 61).

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: García Montero's study of Fujimori as an 'antipolitical' leader describes him as governing through direct, mediated-by-no-one appeals to the masses and against parties and unions.

central-bank-independence.rationale: The 1993 constitution declares the Central Bank autonomous, with monetary stability as its aim (art. 84), although the leadership of the bank was replaced in the 1992 coup.

death-penalty.rationale: The 1993 constitution extended the death penalty to terrorism (and treason in wartime) (art. 140).

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: The constitution has the President of the Republic elected by direct suffrage (art. 111).

direct-votes.rationale: Article 32 lets citizens decide by referendum on binding rules, constitutional amendment and decentralisation, and the 1993 constitution itself was put to a referendum.

elective-rulers.rationale: The constitution has the President of the Republic elected by direct suffrage, with a run-off if nobody wins an absolute majority (art. 111).

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Article 137 lets the President decree a state of emergency in which personal freedom, home inviolability and freedom of assembly and movement are suspended, and Fujimori put about 80% of the territory under emergency.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Article 2 gives everyone the right to equality before the law, with no discrimination for origin, race, sex, language, religion, opinion or economic situation.

filial-duty.rationale: Article 6 says children have the duty to respect and aid their parents.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: The constitution puts foreigners in the same position as Peruvians on property, barring them from acquiring land only within 50 km of the borders (art. 71).

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: The government gave priority to foreign investment and privatised to investors, and the constitution subjects national and foreign investment to the same conditions (art. 63).

head-commands-forces.rationale: The constitution makes the President Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces and the National Police (art. 167), and García Montero notes it left military promotions to the President.

head-of-state-dissolves-parliament.rationale: He dissolved Congress in 1992 and the 1993 constitution gave the President the power to dissolve it after two censured cabinets (art. 134).

indigenous-internal-justice.rationale: Article 149 lets the authorities of rural and native communities, with peasant patrols, exercise jurisdiction under their customary law, within fundamental rights.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The government left prices to the market, privatised and opened trade, and the constitution makes private initiative free within a social market economy with the State in a subsidiary business role (arts. 58, 60).

minority-language-support.rationale: Article 48 makes Quechua, Aymara and other native languages official where they predominate and article 17 requires bilingual and intercultural education.

national-church-status.rationale: Article 50 recognises the Catholic Church as an important element in Peru's formation and lends it cooperation, while other denominations are only respected.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Article 44 lists the State's fundamental duties as including guaranteeing human rights and promoting general welfare, and article 58 has it act on employment, health and education.

one-party-rule.rationale: His regime held contested multi-party elections, in which opposition candidates such as Toledo stood, and the constitution protects political parties and movements (art. 35); no party was given an exclusive right to lead.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Fujimori dissolved Congress in 1992 and legislated by a package of 126 decree-laws, so Congress was not his supreme lawmaking authority.

party-controls-media.rationale: The government censored the main media in 1992 and then controlled the press through tax pressure, judicial threats and Montesinos's bribes.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Article 21 declares historical and cultural assets the cultural heritage of the Nation, protected by the State.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: The 1990 stabilisation programme freed prices and left them to the market instead of fixing them.

price-controls-fight-inflation.rationale: The government fought hyperinflation through austerity and price liberalisation, not price controls.

price-stability-first.rationale: Within two weeks of taking office he launched an austerity programme against hyperinflation, which Britannica credits with stabilising the economy.

property-fundamental.rationale: Article 70 calls the right to property inviolable, guaranteed by the State, with deprivation only for national security or public need and prior cash payment.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Article 70 says the right to property is exercised in harmony with the common good and within the limits of the law.

proportional-representation.rationale: Article 187 provides for proportional representation in multi-party elections, in the form the law sets.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Article 2 gives everyone the right to request information from any public entity without stating a reason and to receive it within the legal term.

public-ownership.rationale: Between 1991 and 1995 much of the public sector was privatised, including state mines and utilities, and the constitution lets the State run businesses only subsidiarily by express law (art. 60).

recall-officials.rationale: Article 31 gives citizens the right to removal or revocation of authorities.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: Roberts reports that the August 1990 shock programme followed president-elect Fujimori's meetings with the IMF, World Bank and Inter-American Development Bank; García Montero adds that the government sought agreement with foreign creditors.

rehabilitation.rationale: The constitution states that the aim of the criminal justice system is reeducation, rehabilitation and reintegration (art. 139), but it also extends the death penalty to terrorism (art. 140).

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Article 46 says no one owes obedience to a government in violation of the constitution and that the civil population has the right to insurrection in defence of the constitutional order.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Article 28 recognises the right to strike but has the law regulate it so it is exercised in harmony with the social interest, with exceptions and limitations.

second-chamber.rationale: The 1993 constitution vests legislative power in a Congress "which has a single chamber" (art. 90).

security-forces-accountable.rationale: In 1995 his government passed an amnesty for all civil, military and police personnel who had committed human-rights violations in 15 years, closing future prosecutions (including the La Cantuta killers).

separate-church-state.rationale: Article 50 makes the Church independent and autonomous but has the State recognise it and cooperate with it, rather than separating the two strictly.

separated-powers.rationale: On 5 April 1992 Fujimori dissolved Congress and the Constitutional Guarantees Tribunal and removed Supreme Court judges and the electoral authority, and later dismissed judges who ruled his third term unconstitutional.

single-official-language.rationale: Article 48 makes Quechua, Aymara and other native languages official alongside Spanish wherever they predominate.

social-market-economy.rationale: Article 58 says private initiative is exercised within a social market economy in which the State acts mainly on employment, health, education, security and public services.

strong-leader.rationale: Britannica reports that Fujimori, frustrated with a legislature that backed few of his programmes, dissolved Congress in April 1992 with military support and then ruled nearly unopposed; García Montero adds that the decision was presented as the only road to order.

suppress-opposition.rationale: On one side the 1992 coup arrested political leaders and journalists, occupied party and union offices and later brought defamation campaigns against critics; on the other the regime kept holding elections that opposition parties contested and won seats in.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Most protective tariffs were eliminated between 1991 and 1995.

torture-always-illegal.rationale: Article 2 states that no one may be subjected to torture or inhuman or humiliating treatment, and that statements obtained by violence are void.

traditional-family.rationale: Article 4 has the community and State protect the family and promote marriage, recognised as natural and fundamental institutions of society.

women-suffrage.rationale: The constitution gives every citizen the vote (art. 31) and bars discrimination on sex (art. 2).

notes: Themes searched: government (separation of powers, Congress, courts, elections, reelection, emergency powers, party competition), economy (privatisation, prices, trade, labour, central bank, investment), society (family, religion, language, indigenous justice), liberty (information, equality, torture, media), world (IMF, foreign investment). Sources read: García Montero (2001), Díaz-Terán (2026), the Roberts article (abstract and notes only), Britannica, the 1993 constitution as amended to 2009, and Fujimori's 1990-2000 messages to Congress (saved, not cited as no statement lacked a record). The Fuerza Popular 2026-2031 plan was read only through a news summary and is not cited. Constitution answers rest on articles the 2009 text keeps from 1993. Wherever the regime has a record the answer follows it; the old Wikipedia-based answers that no source settles are now null.
